title: Working backwards through operations
transcript: Work backwards when you know where an operation ended but need to find where it began. Each step has an inverse that restores its input. For a chain of changes, undo the last change first. Then test the whole forward chain.

An AMC Upper Primary problem may tell you what happened to a mystery number, a balance or a pile and ask for the starting amount. A Rossmoyne style question can also constrain the final range or require whole numbers along the way. Reverse only the legal states.
A machine adds four to a number, then multiplies by four. The final output is forty-four. What went in? Trace from the right of the diagram to the left.

Undo the multiplication by dividing forty-four by four. The result is eleven, just after the original addition. Now subtract four to find the input seven. As a check, forward addition and multiplication return forty-four.

Remove one of three equal parts of a pile. Then add six counters. There are twenty-two counters afterwards. How many were in the pile at the start? Write the intermediate state before restoring the whole.

Subtract the addition of six. That leaves sixteen, which is two of the original three equal parts. Divide those sixteen counters by two. One original part has eight counters. Rebuild the original three parts. There were twenty-four counters before either operation.

Start with a positive whole number. Add three, multiply by five, divide by two, and subtract five. The final reading is a whole number from twenty-five to thirty-five inclusive. Find all possible whole-number inputs.

Take each possible reading, add five, then multiply by two. We are undoing the final two operations. An input can be whole only if that intermediate result is divisible by five. Check the readings against this condition before going further. The allowed readings are twenty-five, thirty and thirty-five. Undo the first two operations for those readings only.

Divide each allowed intermediate value by five, then subtract three. This gives nine, eleven and thirteen. For example, starting at nine and running all four steps forward gives twenty-five. Every reading in the requested interval was tested.

Undo multiplication with division, and undo addition with subtraction. Reversing just the signs without reversing the order changes the input. A fraction refers to the whole at the time it was used. Check how many equal parts the intermediate value represents.

Write a short arrow for every step. Work from the known output, writing the inverse of the last arrow first. Check required whole numbers and allowed ranges as you reverse. Confirm your answer by running each claimed input forward.
